state.case_summary:
A 50-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with a 1-week history of rapidly progressive gait disturbance. He reported no back pain, fevers, night sweats, or weight loss and had no history of smoking or known malignancy. On examination, he had full strength throughout all extremities but had decreased sensation from the T3 dermatome downward. He exhibited four beats of clonus bilaterally, hyperreflexia in the lower extremities, and profound ataxia, rendering him unable to walk more than a few steps. 

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated a diffusely enhancing lesion centered at T1 with near-circumferential epidural extension causing severe cord compression. CT of the thoracic spine showed an expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements. CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no evidence of a primary malignancy, and laboratory studies, including inflammatory markers, were within normal limits. 

Given his rapidly progressive neurological decline, the decision was made to proceed urgently with surgical decompression, spinal stabilization, and tissue diagnosis.
